turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files describing perovskite solar cells as
complete devices — `substrate` (glass + transparent electrode), `etl`
(electron-transport layer stack), `htl` (hole-transport layer stack),
`backcontact` (metal / carbon back electrode), `deposition` (absorber
deposition procedure; `>>` separates steps). Every candidate below uses the
same MAPbI3 absorber in the same n-i-p (regular) architecture; they differ
only in the remaining columns. Each row is a device CONFIGURATION whose
efficiency is the median over at least 3 independently fabricated cells, so
it is a reproducible recipe rather than a single champion cell:
  - b3_pvk_stack_train.csv: 300 configurations with the measured power
    conversion efficiency (%).
  - b3_pvk_stack_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE configurations whose power
    conversion efficiency (%) was NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and
    the same device columns.

Using the training data, select the 5 candidates with the HIGHEST power
conversion efficiency (%).

Reason from the device physics — band alignment and selectivity of the
transport layers, interface recombination, contact chemistry and the film
quality the process is likely to give — then end your answer with an
explicit ranked list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902,
c903, c904, c905".
turns.answer_text:
# Device Physics Analysis

Looking at the training data, several strong efficiency drivers emerge:

**ETL chemistry:** SnO2-based ETLs (SnO2-c, SnO2-np) consistently outperform TiO2-only stacks. SnO2 has better electron mobility, wider bandgap, and lower trap density than TiO2, giving better electron extraction and less UV-induced degradation. The single highest efficiency in the training set (20.85%) uses a **TiO2-c | SnO2-np** bilayer ETL — the thin compact TiO2-c layer blocks pinholes/shunting while the SnO2-np layer boosts electron selectivity.

**HTL chemistry:** Spiro-MeOTAD remains the benchmark HTL (good HOMO alignment with MAPbI3, ~-5.2 eV), but PTAA also correlates strongly with high efficiency in this dataset (12.4–18.9%) due to its lower trap density and better hydrophobicity that improves perovskite crystallization on top.

**Back contact:** Au and Ag dominate the top of the training distribution; MoO3 interlayers (MoO3|Ag, MoO3|Au) improve hole extraction by reducing the HTL/metal barrier and preventing metal diffusion into the HTL.

**Interpretation of candidates:**
- **c064** (TiO2-c | SnO2-np, Spiro-MeOTAD, Au) is an almost exact structural analog of the single best training recipe (20.85%), differing only in back contact metal (Au vs Ag) — both are excellent hole-blocking, low-resistance contacts to Spiro-MeOTAD.
- **c068** (SnO2-np | TiO2-np, PTAA, Au|MoO3) combines two independently strong predictors (SnO2-based ETL + PTAA HTL) with a MoO3-buffered Au contact for improved hole extraction.
- **c021** (SnO2-np | CPTA, Spiro-MeOTAD, Au) again pairs the high-performing SnO2-np ETL with the reliable Spiro-MeOTAD/Au combination; CPTA is a known passivating interlayer that can reduce interfacial recombination.
- **c077** (SnO2-np, Spiro-MeOTAD, Au) is a clean, minimal-defect analog of training recipes in the 14% bracket, but the flexible PEN|ITO substrate here is paired with a very "clean" SnO2/Spiro/Au system, which in this dataset's high-performing subset consistently reaches the upper efficiency range.
- **c035** (SnO2-np, Spiro-MeOTAD, MoO3|Ag|WO3) leverages the SnO2/Spiro combination with a MoO3-buffered back contact, mirroring several 16–17.5% training entries with MoOx-buffered metal contacts.

These five recipes combine the most consistently favorable ETL (SnO2 family), HTL (Spiro-MeOTAD/PTAA), and back-contact (Au/Ag with optional MoO3 buffering) motifs seen at the top of the training distribution, while avoiding known poor performers (mesoporous carbon stacks, ZnO-nw, exotic single-layer ETLs, "none" layers).

Final: c064, c068, c021, c077, c035
